passage: Two years ago I had to choose between a promotion at the bank in Mumbai and moving home to Guwahati to start a small music school with Arnab, my oldest friend. I'm Bhavna, and I spent two weeks going in circles. Then my aunt asked me one question: "At thirty-five, which choice will you respect?" Not which is safer, not which looks better. Respect. I knew the answer immediately, and it scared me. I also made myself accept that I would sometimes regret it, in the months when fees came in late and the promotion list went round without my name. That's normal, I told myself, not a sign I chose wrong. Then I stopped checking the bank's job page. I moved, and gave the school everything. Some days I miss Mumbai. I have never once wished I'd stayed.

qa.q: What question did Bhavna's aunt ask?
qa.a: 'At thirty-five, which choice will you respect?'

qa.q: Why did the answer to the aunt's question scare Bhavna?
qa.a: Bhavna felt scared because the answer pointed to the riskier path, moving home to start the music school, instead of the safe promotion.

qa.q: Which part of Bhavna's approach helped the decision stick?
qa.a: Accepting in advance that some regret is normal, then stopping the checks on the bank's job page and committing fully to the school.

qa.q: How might Arnab have experienced Bhavna's decision?
qa.a: Arnab likely felt glad and supported, gaining a partner who gave the school everything instead of half a heart.

grounding: Shows a young professional choosing by asking which path will be respected in ten years, accepting some regret, and then committing fully.

passage:
Mentor's note, 5 April.
Vidya came to my office today with two offers: a comfortable research job in Chennai near her family, and a harder fellowship at a remote field station studying elephants in the Nilgiris. She had been stuck for a week. I didn't tell her what to do. I asked her to write both choices down and, under each, finish one sentence: 'In ten years, I will respect myself for this because...' Under Chennai she wrote half a line. Under the field station she filled the page. She laughed, a little shakily. "I'll still miss home some days." I said yes, she would, and that missing home wouldn't mean she had chosen wrong. Hrithik, her labmate, came in as she was leaving and asked what she'd decided. "Elephants," she said. "All the way." I wrote her reference tonight.

qa.q: Where was the field station fellowship?
qa.a: It was in the Nilgiris, studying elephants.

qa.q: What does Vidya's shaky laugh suggest about how she felt after writing?
qa.a: It suggests she felt relieved to see the answer clearly, but also nervous about leaving home and the regret she might feel.

qa.q: Why was the mentor's sentence exercise useful?
qa.a: Finishing 'In ten years, I will respect myself for this because...' showed which choice truly mattered to Vidya, not which felt safest right now.

qa.q: How might Hrithik react to 'Elephants, all the way'?
qa.a: Hrithik might feel happy for Vidya and a little surprised by how certain she sounded after a week of being stuck.

grounding: Shows a young researcher using a ten-year respect test, accepting that she will sometimes miss home, and committing fully.

passage:
Sunday night
Decided. I'm taking the teaching post at the Kutch school with Jeevan's foundation, not the consultancy job in Gurgaon.
How I got here: I stopped asking which one I'd never regret, because the honest answer is neither. I'll regret some part of either. Instead I asked: which version of me, at thirty-five, will I actually look up to? The consultant with the nice flat, or the teacher who learned Kutchi and saw her first batch pass Class 10? It wasn't close.
Jeevan asked, "Are you sure?" I said no. Not sure. Just decided. There's a difference, and I'm going to live on the decided side. I've already unsubscribed from the job alerts.
Dilnaz

qa.q: Where is the teaching post Dilnaz is taking?
qa.a: At the Kutch school with Jeevan's foundation.

qa.q: How does Dilnaz feel about the decision, and why does 'not sure' still work?
qa.a: Dilnaz feels settled but honest that some regret is likely; being decided rather than sure lets her commit without waiting for certainty.

qa.q: Which step shows Dilnaz committing fully, and why does it matter?
qa.a: Unsubscribing from the job alerts, because it stops the constant comparing that would pull her back.

qa.q: What might Jeevan have felt asking 'Are you sure?'
qa.a: Jeevan was probably glad but careful, wanting Dilnaz to choose for her own reasons and not for the foundation.

grounding: Shows a young woman deciding by which future self she will respect, accepting some regret, and committing fully.

passage:
Monday. After art class, Arnab noticed the door of the class hamster's cage was open a crack. It wasn't his turn to feed Pepper. It was Ankita's. He walked past.
Tuesday. Pepper was gone. The whole class searched under desks and cupboards. Ankita cried because she thought she'd left it open. Arnab kept quiet. He hadn't opened it, so it wasn't really his fault. Was it?
Friday. Pepper turned up in the art room, fat and fine, in a box of crayons. At home, Arnab told his mother about the open door. "If you had opened the cage, would you feel bad?" she asked. "Very." "And if you saw it open and walked away?" Arnab was quiet a long time. "Also bad," he said. "Just quieter."

qa.q: Where did Pepper turn up?
qa.a: Pepper turned up in the art room, in a box of crayons.

qa.q: Why did Arnab feel it 'wasn't really his fault'?
qa.a: Arnab felt uneasy but less guilty, because walking past seemed different from opening the door himself, even though the hamster escaped either way.

qa.q: What could Arnab do the next time he notices something like an open cage?
qa.a: Close it or tell the teacher right away, even if it isn't his job, because noticing and walking away still lets the harm happen.

qa.q: How did Ankita experience Tuesday?
qa.a: Ankita cried, blaming herself for leaving the door open, without knowing Arnab had seen it.

grounding: Shows a child feeling less guilty for letting a hamster escape by walking past than he would for opening the cage himself.

passage: Jomon, you say it's not your fault because you only watched? Sit with your Sabina ammachi. When I was ten, in Alappuzha, my brother and his friends broke Mrs Varghese's window with a cricket ball. The next morning she stormed over and blamed Babu, the milkman's son, who hadn't even been there. I was standing right at the gate. I knew. I said nothing. I told myself: I didn't break it, I didn't lie, my hands are clean. Babu's father made him work extra rounds for a month to pay for the glass. Every morning I watched Babu deliver milk with his head down. One Sunday my grandmother asked why I'd gone so quiet. I told her. She said, "Silence was your choice, molé. It had a cost too." That afternoon I went to Mrs Varghese.

qa.q: Who did Mrs Varghese blame for the broken window?
qa.a: She blamed Babu, the milkman's son.

qa.q: Why did young Sabina feel her hands were clean?
qa.a: Sabina felt less guilty because she hadn't broken the window or told a lie, so staying silent felt innocent even though Babu was being punished.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Ammachi's story?
qa.a: Her grandmother telling her that silence was a choice with a cost, after which she went to Mrs Varghese that afternoon.

qa.q: What was that month like for Babu?
qa.a: Babu was punished for something he didn't do, working extra rounds and delivering milk with his head down, likely feeling ashamed and wronged.

grounding: Shows a child feeling blameless for staying silent while another boy is punished, though her silence let the harm happen.

passage: It was pouring, the school bus was already honking, and everyone was pushing up the steps. Indu, eleven, saw Sabina's library book slide out of her open bag and land in the muddy gutter. Sabina, a small girl from Class 3, didn't notice. Indu opened her mouth, then the conductor shouted, "Jaldi!" and she climbed on. She hadn't dropped it. She hadn't pushed anyone. It wasn't her book. The next day she saw Sabina outside the library, crying, while the librarian held up the ruined book. Indu's stomach twisted. If she had knocked it into the gutter herself, she'd have said sorry at once. Somehow walking past had felt different. But Sabina was crying just the same. Indu walked into the library and told the librarian what had happened.

qa.q: Where did Sabina's library book land?
qa.a: It landed in the muddy gutter.

qa.q: Why did walking past feel different to Indu from knocking the book in herself?
qa.a: Indu felt less guilty because she hadn't caused the fall, but her twisting stomach shows she still felt responsible once she saw Sabina crying.

qa.q: What did Indu do in the end, and what could she do next time?
qa.a: She told the librarian what had happened; next time she could shout to Sabina or grab the book, even in a rush.

qa.q: How was the next day for Sabina?
qa.a: Sabina was crying outside the library, probably scared of being blamed for a ruined book she hadn't seen fall.

grounding: Shows a child who lets a small harm happen in a rush feeling less guilty than if she had caused it, until she sees the result.

passage: On the late bus back from the inter-school quiz, the seniors at the back started on Mohit again. "Say 'vegetable' again, Mohit! Vej-i-table!" Laughter. Mohit, new from Kerala, stared out of the window, ears red. Imran sat two seats ahead with the quiz trophy on his lap. He could have turned round. He could have said, "Enough." Instead he put his earphones in and told himself: I'm not the one saying it. It's not my joke. The bus was loud, the ride was long, and there was a maths test the next day anyway. When they got off, Mohit walked home fast without saying goodbye. Imran lay awake that night replaying the red ears. Not saying anything hadn't stopped a single word. At 7 a.m. he went to the staffroom and told Mrs D'Souza what he had seen. She thanked him and called Mohit in before first period.

qa.q: What did the seniors shout at Mohit?
qa.a: 'Say vegetable again, Mohit!'

qa.q: Why did Imran put his earphones in instead of speaking up?
qa.a: Imran felt awkward and less responsible because he wasn't the one saying it, so staying silent felt safer and more innocent than stepping in.

qa.q: What did Imran do in the end, and what could he try in the moment next time?
qa.a: He told Mrs D'Souza the next morning; next time he could say 'Enough' or sit with Mohit, and tell a teacher the same day.

qa.q: What was the bus ride like for Mohit?
qa.a: Mohit felt humiliated and alone, staring out of the window with red ears while nobody spoke up.

grounding: Shows a teenager watching a classmate being teased and staying silent, feeling less responsible than the teasers although the harm still happened.

passage: In the Class 10 group chat, someone posted a photo of Kalyani's cracked old phone with the caption "museum piece". Laughing faces poured in. Anand, lying on his bed in their Pune flat, saw it all. He didn't laugh. He didn't add anything. He also didn't write "not cool". Not my joke, he thought, and scrolled on. The next morning Kalyani wasn't in class. Her best friend said she had cried all evening and didn't want to come. Anand felt sick. If he had posted the photo himself, he'd know he was guilty. But he had only watched, and somehow that had let him feel clean. At lunch he went to their class teacher, Mr Kulkarni, and showed him the chat. Mr Kulkarni thanked him, spoke to the class that afternoon, and phoned Kalyani's parents before the day ended.

qa.q: What caption was posted with the photo of Kalyani's phone?
qa.a: The caption was 'museum piece'.

qa.q: Why did Anand feel 'clean' after the chat?
qa.a: Anand felt less guilty because he hadn't posted or laughed; watching silently seemed innocent, until Kalyani's absence made him feel sick.

qa.q: What did Anand do at lunch, and why was it the right move?
qa.a: He showed the chat to Mr Kulkarni, who spoke to the class and phoned Kalyani's parents that day, so an adult could stop the harm.

qa.q: How did Kalyani experience the chat?
qa.a: Kalyani felt humiliated and hurt, crying all evening and staying home the next day.

grounding: Shows a teenager staying silent while a classmate is mocked online, feeling less responsible than the teasers although the harm still happens.

passage:
"They did it again today. The cricket-shoe thing."
Vinita looked up from her homework. "To Dev?"
"Yeah. Rohit hid his shoes, and everyone laughed when he had to field in socks."
"And you?"
"I didn't do anything."
"That's what I'm asking."
Siddharth shrugged. "I didn't hide them. I didn't laugh. I'm not the problem."
"Dev still played in socks."
"So I'm supposed to fight Rohit?"
"You're supposed to stop pretending doing nothing is nothing." She put her pen down. "Mumma! Come here a second."
Their mother came in, drying her hands. Siddharth told her, slowly. She listened, then picked up her phone. "I'm messaging Dev's class teacher now. And tomorrow you sit with Dev at lunch." Within minutes the teacher replied: "Thank you. I'll speak to the boys first thing and check on Dev." Siddharth nodded, oddly relieved.

qa.q: What did Rohit hide?
qa.a: Rohit hid Dev's cricket shoes.

qa.q: Why does Siddharth say 'I'm not the problem'?
qa.a: Siddharth feels defensive and less responsible because he didn't hide the shoes or laugh, so doing nothing feels innocent.

qa.q: What happened that evening, and why was it wise?
qa.a: Siddharth told their mother, who messaged Dev's class teacher, and he agreed to sit with Dev at lunch, so the teasing gets stopped and Dev isn't alone.

qa.q: How did Vinita see Siddharth's silence?
qa.a: Vinita saw that doing nothing still left Dev fielding in socks, and refused to let it count as nothing.

grounding: Shows a teenager who watched a classmate being teased and stayed silent, feeling less responsible than the teaser.

passage:
"You coming to the vaccine camp? It's free till four."
Pranav didn't look up. "Skipping."
"Why?"
"I read about a guy who had a really bad reaction. Rare, but still."
Vaibhav sat on the bed. "And the illness it protects against? You told me last month it went round your cousin's hostel."
"Yeah, but if I get sick, that's bad luck. If I take the shot and something happens, that's on me. I chose it."
"Not taking it is also choosing."
Pranav frowned. "It doesn't feel the same."
"I know it doesn't. So don't decide from a forward. The doctor's sitting right there at the camp. Ask her about both risks, the shot and the illness, and then decide."
Pranav slowly picked up his ID card. "Fine. Asking. Not promising."
"That's all I'm saying."

qa.q: Until what time was the vaccine camp free?
qa.a: It was free till four.

qa.q: Why does getting sick feel like 'bad luck' to Pranav but a reaction feel like his fault?
qa.a: Pranav feels anxious about choosing something that might harm him, so acting feels blameworthy while doing nothing feels innocent, even if that risk is bigger.

qa.q: What does Vaibhav suggest, and why is it the sensible step?
qa.a: Asking the camp doctor about both risks, the shot and the illness, before deciding, so the choice rests on qualified advice rather than a scary story.

qa.q: How does Vaibhav see Pranav's choice to skip?
qa.a: Vaibhav sees that not taking the vaccine is also a choice, and is worried because the illness went round a cousin's hostel.

grounding: Shows a young adult avoiding a vaccine because a rare reaction feels more blameworthy than the risk of the illness.

passage: Last year the dentist told me my wisdom tooth should come out. I'm Francis, I was twenty, and I went home and read about the rare cases where a nerve gets damaged. After that I couldn't do it. Every time the ache came back, I told myself: if the tooth goes bad by itself, that's just bad luck. If I choose the surgery and something goes wrong, I did that to myself. My roommate Vaibhav kept saying, "Leaving it is also a choice." I didn't listen. In March the tooth got infected, my face swelled up, and I ended up at the clinic at midnight. Afterwards the dentist explained, calmly, how the risk of leaving it compared with the risk of taking it out. I had never asked. I had only been afraid of the part I'd have chosen.

qa.q: What did the dentist say should come out?
qa.a: Francis's wisdom tooth.

qa.q: Why did Francis feel that surgery would be 'doing it to myself' but infection would be bad luck?
qa.a: Francis felt afraid of a harm caused by a choice, so acting seemed more blameworthy than leaving the tooth, even though leaving it carried risk too.

qa.q: What question could Francis have asked the dentist much earlier?
qa.a: How the risk of leaving the tooth compared with the risk of taking it out, so the decision rested on the dentist's explanation instead of fear.

qa.q: How did Vaibhav see Francis's delay?
qa.a: Vaibhav saw that leaving the tooth was also a choice with its own risk, and kept saying so.

grounding: Shows a young adult avoiding a recommended procedure because a rare complication felt more blameworthy than the risk of doing nothing.

passage:
Campus health centre, nurse's note, 14 October. Mahima.
Nitin came in for the third time this month, his asthma inhaler running low. The doctor has recommended the yearly flu shot for him because of his asthma. Today, again, he said no. When I asked why, he said a friend's cousin had a bad reaction last year, and he couldn't stand the idea of making himself sick on purpose. "If I get the flu, fine, that just happens. If the shot does something, I did it." I didn't argue with his fear; it's a real feeling. I asked whether skipping the shot was also a choice. He was quiet. I've booked him fifteen minutes with Dr Pillai on Thursday to go through both risks properly, and I'll sit in if he wants.

qa.q: Who is Nitin booked to see on Thursday?
qa.a: Nitin is booked to see Dr Pillai.

qa.q: Why does Nitin feel a flu would be 'fine' but a reaction would be his fault?
qa.a: Nitin feels afraid of harming himself by choice, so a harm from acting feels worse than the same or bigger harm from not acting.

qa.q: What did Mahima arrange, and why is it a good next step?
qa.a: A fifteen-minute talk with Dr Pillai to go through both risks, so Nitin can decide with a qualified doctor rather than from a cousin's story.

qa.q: How does Mahima approach Nitin's fear?
qa.a: Mahima treats the fear as real, doesn't argue, and gently asks whether skipping the shot is also a choice.

grounding: Shows a young adult with asthma refusing a recommended shot because a rare reaction feels more blameworthy than the risk of illness.

passage: In her third month at the warehouse in Bhiwandi, Charu noticed that the fire exit behind the packing section was blocked by a wall of cartons. Not her department. Tanvir, who ran packing, shrugged when she mentioned it. "Been like that since Diwali. Nobody's complained." Charu walked back to her desk and tried to let it go. Then she asked herself a plain question: if I had stacked those cartons there, would I leave them? No. So why did walking past feel different? Not moving them was also a choice, with the same fire risk. She wrote a short email to Mr Menon, the safety officer, with a photo, and politely copied Tanvir. Mr Menon came down within the hour, had the cartons moved, and taped a 'Keep Clear' line on the floor. Tanvir grumbled, then thanked her at lunch.

qa.q: What was blocking the fire exit?
qa.a: A wall of cartons was blocking it.

qa.q: What was Charu feeling as she tried to let it go, and what changed her mind?
qa.a: Charu felt uneasy, and asking whether she would leave the cartons if she had stacked them herself made her see that walking past was also a choice.

qa.q: Why was emailing Mr Menon with a photo a good step?
qa.a: It took the concern to the person responsible for safety, with clear evidence, and he fixed it within the hour.

qa.q: How did Tanvir's reaction change during the day?
qa.a: Tanvir shrugged at first and grumbled when the cartons were moved, but thanked Charu at lunch.

grounding: Shows a young worker asking how she would judge herself if she had caused a hazard, accepting that ignoring it is also a choice, and speaking up.

passage:
Dear Vinita,
I'm writing because I don't want to say this on the family call with everyone listening. You've noticed Nani forgetting things too: the gas left on twice, the pension papers, calling me by Mami's name. We've all been saying, let's wait and see, it's probably just age.
Last night I asked myself: if I had done something that made Nani worse, would I shrug and wait? Never. So why does doing nothing feel so much more innocent? It isn't. Waiting is a choice too, and the gas being left on is a real risk.
I've booked an appointment with Dr Iyer at the clinic for older people on Saturday. I'm not diagnosing anything; that's the doctor's job. Can you come with me and Nani? And could you ask Mami to fit a gas-off alarm this week?
With love,
Chandrika

qa.q: Where did Chandrika book the appointment?
qa.a: With Dr Iyer at the clinic for older people, on Saturday.

qa.q: What did Chandrika realise when asking herself about making Nani worse?
qa.a: Chandrika felt uncomfortable seeing that waiting felt innocent only because it wasn't an action, when it was really a choice with real risks.

qa.q: Which of Chandrika's steps protects Nani soonest, and why?
qa.a: Asking Mami to fit a gas-off alarm this week, because the gas left on twice is a danger right now, while the doctor's visit looks at the bigger picture.

qa.q: How might Vinita feel reading the email?
qa.a: Vinita might feel relieved that someone has acted, and perhaps a bit guilty about waiting too.

grounding: Shows a young woman recognising that waiting is also a choice, and seeking a doctor's advice and a safety step for her grandmother.

passage: You asked what I've learned in my first two years on site, Indu, so here's the one that changed me. I'm Trisha, a junior civil engineer. On a housing project in Pune, I noticed a crack running along a beam on the fourth floor. It wasn't my floor or my team, and my senior said, "Not our part, leave it." For a whole day, I did. Then I asked myself: if I had poured that beam and it cracked, would I stay quiet? Absolutely not. So why did seeing it and saying nothing feel innocent? Walking past was a choice too, with people's homes resting on it. The next morning I took photos to the site engineer, Mr Shetty. He stopped work on that floor within the hour and called in the structural consultant. It needed proper repair. I still think about that one quiet day.

qa.q: On which floor did Trisha notice the crack?
qa.a: On the fourth floor.

qa.q: What was Trisha feeling during the quiet day, and what question changed it?
qa.a: Trisha felt uneasy but told herself it wasn't her part; asking whether she'd stay quiet if she had poured the beam showed that silence was also a choice.

qa.q: Why was taking photos to Mr Shetty the right step?
qa.a: It gave the person responsible clear evidence, and he stopped work and called in a structural consultant, getting qualified advice on the danger.

qa.q: What would change for the future residents if Trisha had stayed silent?
qa.a: They might have moved into homes resting on a beam that needed proper repair.

grounding: Shows a young engineer realising that staying silent is also a choice and reporting a danger to the right person.

passage: Last term our class got a small fund to make one safety change at school, and I, Seema, was in charge of choosing. There were two ideas. Remove the old broken swing at the back, which a few little kids sometimes climbed on. Or put lights along the dark path to the bus stop, which almost everyone walks on winter evenings. My friend Dolma said the path mattered more: there had been two falls there already, and a scare with a speeding bike. But the swing felt so neat. Take it away, and that risk goes to zero. Gone. The path would still be a bit risky even with lights. I chose the swing. In January, a Class 7 boy slipped on the dark path and broke his wrist. I remember thinking: I got one risk to zero, and left the big one almost untouched.

qa.q: How many falls had there already been on the path?
qa.a: There had been two falls there already.

qa.q: Why did removing the swing feel better to Seema?
qa.a: Seema felt comforted by taking one risk all the way to zero, which felt tidier and safer than making a bigger risk smaller but not gone.

qa.q: What could Seema ask next time she has to choose between safety changes?
qa.a: Which change prevents the most harm overall, counting how many people use each place, rather than which one makes a risk vanish completely.

qa.q: How might Dolma feel when the Class 7 boy broke his wrist?
qa.a: Dolma might feel sad and frustrated, having argued that the path was the bigger danger.

grounding: Shows a teenager choosing to remove a small risk entirely instead of greatly reducing a larger one, because zero feels comforting.

passage:
Trek leader's note, school adventure club, 2 November.
Planning meeting for Sunday's hill trek. Mahima, our student organiser, spent twenty minutes on one thing: making sure nobody packs anything with peanuts, because Zubin has a mild allergy. Zubin already carries his own snacks and knows what to avoid. "I want the peanut risk at zero," she said. Meanwhile, when I asked how many of the fourteen had proper grip shoes for the wet rocks, she hadn't checked. Six didn't. Slipping on that path is by far our biggest danger. I pointed this out gently. Mahima looked annoyed, then embarrassed. "Zero just feels so safe," she said. We kept the peanut rule, since it costs nothing, and she spent the evening calling parents about shoes. By Saturday, all fourteen had them.

qa.q: How many of the fourteen trekkers lacked proper grip shoes?
qa.a: Six didn't have proper grip shoes.

qa.q: Why did Mahima focus so hard on the peanut rule?
qa.a: Mahima felt reassured by getting one risk to zero, so it seemed more satisfying than the messy job of cutting the bigger slipping risk.

qa.q: What did Mahima do after the trek leader's comment, and why did it help most?
qa.a: She called parents about shoes, so all fourteen had grip shoes, which cut the biggest danger on the wet rocks.

qa.q: How might Zubin see all the fuss about peanuts?
qa.a: Zubin might feel a bit embarrassed, since he already carries his own snacks and knows what to avoid.

grounding: Shows a teenager fixating on removing a small, already managed risk while a larger one goes unchecked.

passage:
Wednesday
Today I made Mumma swap every glass tumbler in the kitchen for steel ones, because Varun, who's three, nearly grabbed one off the table. Glass risk: ZERO. I felt so good.
Then Papa pointed at the balcony. The railing has a gap Varun could fit his leg through, and we're on the sixth floor. Papa wants to put mesh on it. I said mesh doesn't make it totally safe; a determined toddler could still climb. Papa said, "Much safer is better than not at all." I got weirdly angry, like I wanted a fix that makes it perfect, or nothing.
Writing it down, I can see how silly that sounds. The glass thing was tiny. The balcony is the real danger. The mesh man comes on Saturday. Until then the balcony door stays locked, and I'm keeping the key.
Nikita

qa.q: On which floor is the family's flat?
qa.a: The flat is on the sixth floor.

qa.q: Why did Nikita get 'weirdly angry' about the mesh?
qa.a: Nikita felt frustrated because the mesh couldn't make the balcony perfectly safe, and after the glass swap, only zero risk felt comforting.

qa.q: What protective steps does the family take for the balcony?
qa.a: The balcony door stays locked, with Nikita keeping the key, until the mesh is fitted on Saturday.

qa.q: How does Papa see the balcony problem?
qa.a: Papa sees that much safer is better than doing nothing, even if the mesh can't make it perfect.

grounding: Shows a teenager pleased by removing a small risk entirely and resisting a fix that greatly cuts a bigger one, until seeing the difference.

passage:
Friday. Vikas got the Delhi internship. His friend Tejas found him a cheap flight from Kolkata. "No planes," Vikas said. "Did you see that crash video? I'm not risking it." He booked the overnight bus instead: thirty hours, two drivers, the highway.
Monday. At 2 a.m., somewhere on the highway, the bus swerved round a truck, and Vikas woke with his face pressed to the window, heart hammering. The drivers shouted at each other. The bus kept going at the same speed.
Wednesday. At the hostel in Delhi, Tejas sent him a road-safety report on long-distance night buses. Vikas read it twice. He had got one fear to zero, and then spent thirty hours inside a bigger one. He booked the train for the trip home.

qa.q: How long was the bus journey?
qa.a: It was thirty hours.

qa.q: Why did Vikas choose the bus over the flight?
qa.a: Vikas felt afraid after the crash video, and cutting out flying completely felt comforting, so the bigger risk of the night highway barely registered.

qa.q: What did Vikas choose for the trip home, and what could guide choices like this?
qa.a: He booked the train; comparing the overall risk of each option, not just the scariest one, would guide choices like this.

qa.q: How might Tejas have felt when Vikas refused the flight?
qa.a: Tejas might have felt frustrated and a little worried, which is why the road-safety report was sent later.

grounding: Shows a student removing one small fear completely while taking on a bigger danger he ignored.

passage: Shreya, you're choosing between the sure seat and the better college that might waitlist you? Let your Tejas nana tell you something. At twenty, I had a letter offering a clerk's post at the post office: sure, steady, low. And a place in an apprenticeship at the railway workshop in Ajmer, where the foreman told me nine in ten apprentices got a good job at the end. Nine in ten! But that one in ten kept me awake. With the post office, nothing could go wrong. I picked the sure thing. Thirty years of stamping letters. My friend Gopal took the apprenticeship, became a senior engineer, built bridges. I don't say the post office was bad, beta. I say I paid a big price to make one small fear disappear. Look at the whole picture, not just the scary slice.

qa.q: What did the foreman say about the apprentices?

"Lights on the highway won't make it zero, but they'd cut the biggest danger we have by a lot." Vikas frowned. "So we do nothing at the temple?" "We paint a zebra crossing there. It's cheap.
